title: Caching in an interview: when to add a cache, and how to explain it
dek: A cache keeps answers you will need again in memory, so most reads skip the database. It comes up in almost every design with heavy reads, and interviewers listen for two things: that you add it for a reason you can put numbers on, and that you know what it costs. This article is the whole method on one page; the others in this group go deeper into each step.

items: Add a cache only after naming a problem with numbers: too many reads for the database, a slow query, a busy database CPU, or a latency target the database can't meet.
Then walk through five steps: the bottleneck, what to cache and under which key, the pattern (usually cache-aside), eviction and expiry, and what goes wrong.
Don't cache everything. A well-indexed database is often enough, and every cache adds stale data and a new way to fail.

body.x: Why memory is so much faster

Reading one user's profile from Postgres takes a few milliseconds when the row is already in the database's memory, and tens of milliseconds when the query joins several tables or has to wait for the disk under load; reading the same profile from an in-memory store such as Redis takes about one millisecond, network included. That is 5 to 50 times faster, and the gap grows exactly when the database is busiest. The reason is physical: a database keeps its data on disk and pays for disk access on many queries, while memory sits right next to the CPU.

body.cap: The same 12,000 menu reads a second, with and without a cache. With 90% of reads answered from memory, the database sees a tenth of the traffic, and most users wait a millisecond instead of thirty.

body.x: So a cache does two jobs at once: it takes load off the database, and it cuts the time each read takes. It also brings two new problems: keeping the cached copy in step with the database, and surviving the day the cache fails. A good answer covers both sides.
Don't open with a cache. First show the problem it solves. Any of these four is a good reason, and each is stronger with a rough number:

items: Many reads: 'Zotato has 1 crore daily users making about 20 reads each: 20 crore reads a day, around 2,300 a second on average and 12,000 at dinner. Even with indexes, at dinner each takes 10 to 30 ms. A cache answers in under 2 ms and keeps most of them off the database.'
An expensive query: 'The home screen's 'popular near you' list joins orders, restaurants and ratings and takes 200 ms. Compute it once a minute per area, keep it in Redis, and serve it in 1 ms.'
A busy database: 'The database CPU sits at 80% at dinner, almost all of it the same menu queries over and over. Caching them should cut its load by 70 to 80%.'
A latency target: 'The menu API must answer in under 10 ms, and the database takes 30 to 50. A cache is the only way to meet it.'

body.x: The pattern is always the same: name the problem, size it roughly, and say how the cache fixes it. The concept 'Back-of-envelope maths' has the latency numbers worth knowing for databases and caches.
How to introduce it: five steps

body.label: Introducing a cache
head: Step
What to say
Zotato
rows: What exactly is slow or overloaded, with a number
Menu reads: 5,000 a second at dinner, 30 ms each, database CPU at 80%
2. What to cache, and the key
Data read often, changed rarely, costly to fetch or compute
Usually cache-aside; others only for a stated reason
Cache-aside in Redis; a CDN for dish photos
LRU when memory is full; a TTL on every key
allkeys-lru; menus 10 minutes, popular list 60 seconds
One or two failure cases that matter for this system
Delete menu:{id} on edit; coalesce rebuilds of hot keys; survive Redis being down

items: Step 1: point at the specific problem: database load, query time, or an expensive computation. 'Profile reads hit the database 500 times a second at peak, 30 ms each. That's the bottleneck.'

Step 2: not everything belongs in a cache. Good candidates are read often, change rarely, and cost something to fetch: a menu is read on every visit and edited a few times a week. Decide the key too, because the key is how every read finds its entry: user:77:profile, popular:pune-kothrud.

Step 3: match the pattern to how fresh the data must be. 'Cache-aside: read Redis first; on a miss, read the database, store the answer and return it.' Write-through fits when every read must see the latest value and writes can wait; write-behind fits a flood of writes where losing a few is acceptable. Add a CDN if the system serves images or video, and a small in-process cache only for a few extremely hot keys.

Step 4: say how the cache stays within its memory: LRU is the safe default, and a TTL stops entries living forever. 'LRU eviction, a 10-minute TTL on menus, and the entry is deleted the moment a restaurant edits its menu.'

Step 5: show you know the costs. Invalidation: how does a change reach the cache, by deleting on write, by TTL, or by accepting some delay? Failure: if Redis goes down, every read lands on the database; limit that with a circuit breaker and a small local cache. Stampedes: when a popular entry expires, let one request rebuild it while the rest wait (request coalescing), or refresh it a little early.

body.x: Don't list every possible failure. Pick the one or two that matter for the system in front of you and explain how you'd handle them. At a senior level, spend the time on the cases that are important but not obvious, not on things the interviewer can take for granted.

items: If the database copes comfortably with the reads, with the right indexes, a cache only adds a second copy of the truth to keep correct.
If every read is different (a search with free text, a user's own unique report), few reads will ever hit, and the cache wastes memory.
If the data must be exactly current on every read (an account balance before a payment), a cache needs so much care that reading the database is simpler.
Bring up the cache after you have shown a read bottleneck, with numbers.
Say what you cache, the key, the pattern, the eviction policy and the TTL, in that order.
Name one or two things that go wrong and your answer to each; the article 'When caching goes wrong' covers them.
A CDN for static media and an in-process cache for very hot keys are additions, not the first answer.
